title: The RSA Cryptosystem
short: The public key is (n, e) with n = pq; the private key d ≡ e⁻¹ (mod φ(n)); encrypt with c ≡ mᵉ and decrypt with m ≡ cᵈ (mod n).
trouble: Students find d as the inverse of e mod n instead of mod φ(n) = (p − 1)(q − 1).

blocks.html: RSA (Rivest, Shamir and Adleman, 1977) lets anyone encrypt a message to you with a public key, while only you can decrypt it. It is Euler's theorem plus modular inverses plus one fact: multiplying primes is easy, but factoring their product is hard.

items: Setup. Choose primes $p \ne q$. Let $n = pq$ and $\varphi(n) = (p - 1)(q - 1)$.
Encrypt a message $0 \le m < n$: $c = m^{e} \bmod n$. Decrypt: $m = c^{d} \bmod n$.

blocks.html: Since $ed \equiv 1 \pmod{\varphi(n)}$, write $ed = 1 + k\varphi(n)$. If $\gcd(m, n) = 1$, Euler's theorem gives $$c^{d} = m^{ed} = m \cdot \left(m^{\varphi(n)}\right)^{k} \equiv m \cdot 1 = m \pmod{n}.$$ (It also works when $\gcd(m, n) > 1$: check mod $p$ and mod $q$ separately with Fermat, then use the CRT.) Finding $d$ requires $\varphi(n)$, and knowing $\varphi(n) = n - p - q + 1$ is as good as knowing $p$ and $q$. So breaking RSA this way means factoring $n$, which for 600-digit numbers is far out of reach.

blocks.title: Encrypting and decrypting
blocks.q: With $(n, e) = (187, 7)$ and $d = 23$, encrypt $m = 42$, then decrypt.
steps: Decrypt: $15^{23} \bmod 187$ by repeated squaring ($23 = 16 + 4 + 2 + 1$) gives $42$, the original message.

blocks.title: Breaking a tiny key
blocks.q: Eve sees the public key $(n, e) = (187, 7)$. Show how factoring $n$ gives her the private key.
steps: Then $\varphi(187) = 10 \cdot 16 = 160$, and $d = 7^{-1} \bmod 160 = 23$, exactly Alice's private key.
For a 600-digit $n$, the best known factoring methods would run for far longer than the age of the universe on ordinary computers. That gap is the whole security of RSA.

blocks.html: Finding $d$ as the inverse of $e$ mod $n$ instead of mod $\varphi(n)$. Here $7^{-1} \bmod 187 = 107$, and decrypting with it gives $15^{107} \equiv 60 \pmod{187}$, not $42$. The exponent identity comes from Euler's theorem, so exponents work mod $\varphi(n) = (p - 1)(q - 1)$.
Real RSA uses primes with hundreds of digits, $e = 65537$, and a padding scheme that randomizes each message; textbook RSA as above is for understanding, not for protecting secrets.
RSA: $n = pq$, $d \equiv e^{-1} \pmod{(p - 1)(q - 1)}$. Encrypt $c = m^{e}$, decrypt $m = c^{d}$, both mod $n$. Euler's theorem makes them inverse; the difficulty of factoring $n$ keeps $d$ secret.
